title: Three turns, twelve aspects
hookLine: each truth known, its task known, its task done: three turns of four truths (SN 56.11)
carry: no claim until all twelve are clear

cards: A checklist with three columns. Do I know what this is? Do I know what I'm supposed to do with it?

Have I actually done it? Plenty of lines in a life get the first tick and stall there. Near the end of his first sermon, the Buddha describes his own checklist, the one he ran through before he would say he was awakened.

teach.h: THIS IS. TO BE DONE. DONE.
teach.b: For each of the four truths, the Buddha describes knowing it in three turns. The first turn: this is the truth. This is dukkha.
The second: this is what's to be done with it. Dukkha is to be understood. The third: it has been done.
Dukkha has been understood. Then the same three for the arising: this is the arising; it's to be let go; it has been let go. For the ending: to be realized, and realized.
For the path: to be developed, and developed.
Four truths times three turns: twelve aspects. Then the striking line.

The Buddha tells the five monks that as long as his knowledge of these three turns and twelve aspects wasn't fully clear, he didn't claim to be awakened. Only when all twelve were clear did he say it.
That's honesty about his own path, built right into the first sermon. Then the story turns. As the sermon ends, one of the five, Kondañña, sees it.
The sutta says the clear vision arose in him that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease. And the Buddha says, Kondañña has understood.

That, the sutta says, is how he got the name Aññasi Kondañña, Kondañña who understood. The sutta says the gods of the earth shouted that the wheel had been set rolling, and the cry passed up through the heavens.
Some teachers today use the twelve as a map: knowing a truth, knowing its task, and doing it are three different things.

how: The first sermon, with its three turns and twelve aspects, is often chanted in Pali in Theravada monasteries, especially on Asalha Puja, and some teachers use the twelve as a map of practice.

o: each truth known three ways: is, to do, done
three laps around a shrine at a festival
three times the Buddha gave his sermon

games.q: match each turn to what it says.
p: this is what's to be done

s: the Buddha says he claimed awakening before all twelve aspects were clear
he says he didn't claim it until all three turns of all four truths were fully clear.
four truths times three turns makes twelve aspects
this is it, it's to be done, it has been done, for each of the four.
Kondañña's name came to mean Kondañña who understood
the Buddha said Kondañña has understood, and the name stuck.

games.q: the sermon ends. one of the five listeners has seen it. what does the sutta say he saw?
o: that the Buddha was a god.
that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease.
that the world will end soon.
games.why: Kondañña saw that whatever arises is subject to ceasing, and the Buddha said: Kondañña has understood.

practice: Walk the grid in your mind, or draw it if you have paper: four rows for the four truths, three columns, this is, to be done, done.
Move one box per breath, leaving the third column empty, or putting a light mark where you've had even a small taste. No grading; just the shape.

wordCard.voice: Three turns. Each of the four truths known three ways: this is it, this is what's to be done, it has been done. Twelve aspects in all.

orig.note: Pali tiparivaṭṭa: three turns or rounds; the first sermon's three turns of knowing for each truth.

carryVoice: Your line: no claim until all twelve are clear. Knowing a task and doing it are different turns. Three hundred forty-four days in.

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the three turns and twelve aspects; Kondañña's insight
